My brother-in-law Carlos loves to build his own airplanes and fly them.  Nowadays, he is 80 years old. This was his last message to me before he left.
Carlos was born in Mexico, and has a big, beautiful Villa over there in the countryside where we can visit. Now I think I will ride my bicycle there for a short visit.
A message to those who have ears to hear, who are few and far between. People look for recognition and don't care much about these things.
We could do this in Phnom Penh, but use Cambodian flag instead.
Decorate the streets of Siem Reap with bicycles ... but then, someone might steal them.

And many are owned by the city of Rome, evidently acquired from unpaid taxes.

Above and below are examples of the type of graffiti found in Rome.
Probably related to online gaming.
RPD = Rome Police Department. M+S is some sort of petty gang insignia. Be Free.
Drug use = LSD, a synthetic hallucinogenic drug.
420 = marijuana, plus hallucinogenic mushrooms.
Ying yang, balanced duality.
MVCC = Mohawk Valley Community College, which is where I completed my two year post high school degree in the liberal arts. MVCC now owns many aircraft because they have an aviation program.
The aviation program located at the former Griffiss Air Force Base, which is now our local industrial park and the Griffiss International Airport, owned by Oneida County.

During my early teen age years, the USA would send bomber planes like this from Rome to Cambodia. We dropped more bombs on your country than all the bombs dropped during World War II. It was this bombing during the late 1960's that destablized your country, which ultimately led to the rise of the Khmer Rouge.

Lady Liberty - the Statue of Liberty. I recall the sound of these bombers from our home, as they were warming up their engines getting ready to take off and bomb the hell out of your country. After the bombings, our CIA (Central Intelligence Agency) orchestrated the overthrow of your government and put into place Lon Nol - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lon_Nol

But nowadays, the military air force base has been closed down, and it is a very nice business park. The old sign upon entering the air force base back in the 1960's and early 70's ... "Peace is Our Profession" ... "An Equal Opportunity Employer".

"Global Power for America" -- just a short walk from my birth home. Your parents still remember the sounds of the bombs dropping, where all I remember is the sound of the engines warming up. I believe we can setup a cultural exchange program where we can have Cambodian students come here to gain a degree at MVCC.
Here is the MVCC campus, just about one kilometer from my birth home, bordering the old air force base.
They offer several 2 year degree programs ... can't go wrong with liberal arts.
Here's a good degree program ... professional hacker.
Very modern campus with more security cameras than an international airport.
Students are not allowed to commit slow-suicide on campus, but they can still slowly kill themselves off campus.

If you go to school here, this B-52 bomber is nearby to remind you of your homeland. This thing is huge. You can just imagine how your elders felt with it flying over their heads and dropping bombs. Google Street View - https://goo.gl/maps/qhcPGrTniktnW8bR7
Now it's no longer an air force base, but a business and technology park.
About this B-52 bomber ... good thing Cambodian people are a forgiving people.
The business park has a bicycle recycling program.
But nowadays it seems to be shut down.

Urban exploration (often shortened as UE, urbex and sometimes known as roof-and-tunnel hacking) is the exploration of man-made structures, usually abandoned ruins or not usually seen components of the man-made environment. 

Photography and historical interest/documentation are heavily featured in the hobby and, although it may sometimes involve trespassing onto private property, this is not always the case.

Deeper reading:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_exploration

Below are a few photos and commentary from my "Urbex" adventures not far from my birth home.

No one is living here, but it is visited by vandals and looters on a regular basis, I am sure. Upon inspection, the remains in this unit were left by the previous occupant. The refridgerator had been full at the time the electricity was turned off.
Cabinets are of good quality in various states of condition. Kitchen sink is stainless steel deep bowl, good quality fixtures throughout.
Every home is accessable, and in various states of destruction.  Someone had been working to remove this quality fixture ...
whirlpool tubs in all units
quality Delta water mixing fixtures throughout
All units have (or had) water heater, furnace, stove, dishwasher, refridgerator and more.

These units are not being looked after properly. They contain city property which can be salvaged, sold, or redistributed. Property has been left unsecured for looters to help themselves.

As a cross country bicycle tourist, I would have no problem squating here for an extended period of time. Very private and peaceful, and upon selecting and cleaning up an appropriate room, I'd have a really nice place to sleep at night. During the day I'm out and about anyway ...

Do you see Rome there in the middle of New York State? 

Rome is 43 degrees north of the equator, and the elevation is about 120 to 180 meters above sea level (400 to 600 feet).

In the center of Rome is a US National Park, an old reproduction of a miltary fort called "Fort Stanwix."

To the north of Rome are the Adirondack mountains, and to the south are the Catskill mountains and the Finger Lakes region. 

This is a prime area for nature based tourism.

I've salvaged about 25 kilos of potatoes from the garbage, along with oranges, apples, sweet corn, grade A eggs, and much, much more. There is great abundance and waste in Rome, as in all of the United States.
Rome is home to many churches of various denominations.  In the background is Saint Mary's Catholic Church on West Liberty Street.
The Fort Stanwix National Monument managed by the US Park Service is located in the heart of Rome New York. For some strange reason, they fly the flag of the Netherlands as an "open" sign.
This is simply the Visitor's Center on quiet, peaceful summer weekday afternoon.
Plan of Fort Stanwix in 1758

The original fort from the days of the French and Indian War is long gone, but now we have this virtual reproduction. Yes, this National Monument and park is indeed located in the very heart of Rome, New York.
It seems strange, but they don't fly the American flag here at this national monument, rather they fly a variation of red and white stripes, and no blue or stars as seen here. Anyone know why?

The Vistor's Center as pictured earlier above in this photo series, is located at the corner of James Street and Dominick Street. This is the corner where north becomes south and east becomes west, and vice versa.  In other words, it's the center of Rome. In the days of my youth, this corner, which was traditionally called the "American Corner", didn't look this way at all. Our grocery store is located five city blocks to the north, at 506 North James Street. Do you see the survelliance camera? They are everywhere.

This is how the corner did look when I was a boy during the early 1970s.  No such structure such as Fort Stanwix existed at that time except in books and memories. Notice the cupola atop the building. A cupola is a small, round, dome-like structure on top of a building, often used to provide a lookout or to admit light and air.
Here is that same corner today, just at a different angle, but it's the same corner.

A close up of the clock tower in the photo above ... notice there are both audio and video survelliance monitors. Big Brother is watching and listening. Very little crime in Rome, New York.  Police are well funded and are everywhere at all hours. Nice weather too, at least this time of year. Berkshire Hathaway has taken over the country since I've been away. This used to be "The Rome Savings Bank", our family bank.
They call my birthplace, "Historic Rome, New York." This plaque is located on the old "American Corner" as we're discussing above.
Same corner again, the "American Corner" during the 1930s, I presume. Notice the cupola atop the building.
The southwest corner of the American Corner as it is today, the heart of my hometown.
Looking west from the perspective of the Visitor's Center at Fort Stanwix National Monument, the American Corner, Rome New York.

A link to the American Corner through Google Street view.  Not a recent depiction, and if you move around you'll see how construction of the medical businesses has evolved from once being a parking lot. One nice aspect of downtown Rome is that there are no overhead electrical wires. --- https://goo.gl/maps/2Dvd3HXYGBytddZC6 --- in the satellite image above, the "old" American Corner is now the patch of red pavement brick to the left of center.
Historic Rome New York and the old American Corner during the 1930s Great Depression. Notice the cupola atop the building again.

Typographic Fencing defines space and prompts conversation by creating large-scale text in areas where it is not expected - around the edges of parking lots, near ravines, off divided highways. 

These installations are woven out of flagging-tape, a simple, inexpensive material used to mark boundaries. 

Squares in chain-link or vertical-bar fences become pixels on a screen or canvas, the medium for messages. 

Typically, large text is reserved for advertising. 

They are installed anonymously, converting overlooked spaces into landmarks. 

By transforming large-text into large questions, they aim to spark a dialogue. 

Artist/Designer  
Lambchop

https://100.sta-chicago.org/winners/2018/typographic-fencing
